title: Build a task tracker with C#

entryPaths.description: Try each group's readiness task or skip freely. A skip records navigation only.

outcomes.description: Save a short program, read its output, and find the line a compiler error names.
Trace assignments, choose whole-number or fractional division, build text from values, and repair a type mismatch.
Choose a branch with if, comparisons and boolean operators, including the edge values.
Write a static method with parameters and a return value, and explain why a name is out of scope.
Build and walk an array and a List<T> with loops and a running total.
Write a class with properties, a constructor and methods, and predict what two names for one object share.
Tell a copy from a shared reference, change a record with with, and predict == for records, structs and classes.
Mark a value that may be missing with ?, check it before use, and supply a fallback with ?? while keeping zero and empty text.

An empty list returns start. public static double AverageChange(List<int> changes) returns the average of all the changes, negative ones included, keeping any fraction. An empty list returns 0.

The average of no changes must be 0.
Negative changes count in the average: -4 and 4 give 0.

Ana has 2 tasks.

The board must give exactly three keys.
An empty list must give an empty dictionary.

task.title: Readiness 3 · LINQ through exceptions
task.prompt: Update and its record types are supplied. Write public static List<string> Summaries(List<Update> updates). Return one line for each Arrived update, in the form "3 arrived", and one for each Finished update, in the form "Pack: 15 min". Keep the original order. Leave out any other kind of update. A Finished update with negative Minutes is a bug in the data: throw an ArgumentException for it.
hints: Three things can happen to an update: it becomes a line, it is left out, or it is rejected. Which updates get which?
Decide by the update's type, and check the Minutes of a Finished update before building its line.
Loop over the updates. Use is or a switch on the type, throw for Finished with Minutes below 0, and add nothing for other types.

Practice.Summaries(new List<Update> { new Finished("Sort", 0), new Arrived(0) }).SequenceEqual(new List<string> { "Sort: 0 min", "0 arrived" })
ThrowsArgument(() => Practice.Summaries(new List<Update> { new Arrived(1), new Finished("Pack", -1) }))
checkLabels: Arrived and Finished must each give a line, in order, and the Note must be left out.
No updates must give an empty list.
Zero is a real value: "Sort: 0 min" and "0 arrived".
A Finished update with negative Minutes must throw an ArgumentException.
task.feedback: Go through the failing updates one at a time and decide by hand: line, left out, or rejected. Then compare with what your code does.

task.title: Readiness 4 · Generics through tracker
task.prompt: IReader<T> and two readers are supplied. Write two methods. public static async Task<T> ReadOrAsync<T>(IReader<T> reader, T fallback) returns the value the reader reads. When the reader throws InvalidOperationException, it returns the fallback. A value of 0 or an empty string is a real result. public static bool LastOrCheck(Func<List<int>, int, int> candidate) is a check for a candidate that should return the last item of a list, or the given fallback for an empty list. Return true for a correct candidate. Return false for a faulty one that returns the first item, and for one that returns 0 for an empty list whatever the fallback is.
hints: For ReadOrAsync, where does a failed read show up? For LastOrCheck, which inputs make each faulty candidate give a different answer?
A list with two different items exposes first versus last. An empty list with a fallback other than 0 exposes the second bug.
Await the read in a try and return fallback from catch (InvalidOperationException). In the check, compare candidate(list of 4 and 9, 0) with 9 and candidate(empty list, 7) with 7.
checks: Practice.LastOrCheck((items, fallback) => items.Count == 0 ? fallback : items[items.Count - 1]) == true
Practice.LastOrCheck((items, fallback) => items.Count == 0 ? fallback : items[0]) == false
checkLabels: A reader holding 5 must give 5.
The same method must work for a reader of strings.
An offline reader must give the fallback.
A value of 0 is a real result, not a failure.
A correct candidate must pass your check.
A candidate that returns the first item must fail your check.
A candidate that returns 0 for an empty list must fail your check.
task.feedback: For the reader, compare an offline reader with one that holds 0. For the check, find an input where each faulty candidate gives a different answer from a correct one.

lessons.title: Save, run, read output

outcomes.can: Predict the lines a short program prints, in order.
Find the line a compiler error names and repair it.
Print an exact two-line message from a written description.

lessons.intro: Every exercise in this course works the same way: you edit a file, save it, and read what comes back. This module covers that loop: printing a line, reading the output, and reading a compiler error.

steps.title: Save a file and read its output
steps.text: A C# program is a list of statements that run from top to bottom. Console.WriteLine("Ready"); is one statement. It prints the text between the double quotes, then ends the line. The semicolon ends the statement. When you save an exercise, the checker compiles your code, runs it, and compares the result with what the task asked for. Compiling means the C# compiler reads the whole file first. If it finds an error, nothing runs.

steps.title: Predict before running
steps.text: Read the example and predict its output before you run it.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.text: The two statements ran in the order they were written, and each printed on its own line. The quotes mark where the text starts and stops. They are not printed. Output must match exactly: capital letters, spaces and punctuation all count.

steps.title: Predict a compiler error
steps.text: One statement in this example is not finished. Read it before checking.

steps.title: Read the compiler error
steps.text: Check the example. The compiler reports CS1002: ; expected. The numbers in brackets after the file name are the line and the column where it noticed the problem. Line 1 has no semicolon, so nothing ran, not even line 2. Every compiler error has a code such as CS1002 and names a line. Start reading at that line.

steps.title: Repair the first message
steps.text: Save the starter as it is and read the error. Fix that line, save again, and compare the output with the prompt.

steps.title: Print the board sign
steps.text: Work from the prompt. Save to check your output.

choices.feedback: Each Console.WriteLine prints its text and ends the line.
Console.WriteLine ends the line after its text, so the next print starts a new line.
Statements run from top to bottom, in the order they are written.

choices.text: It prints Ready and Open, because line 2 is complete.

lessons.title: Values, types and text

outcomes.can: Predict the order and values printed after an update.
Choose between whole-number and fractional division.
Build text from supplied values.
Read a type mismatch error and repair the variable's type.
Use an inferred variable and keep a count correct across an update in a new setting.

lessons.intro: A program keeps its data in named variables. In C# every variable has a type that says what kind of value it can hold. This module covers whole numbers, numbers with a fraction, text and true/false values, and the arithmetic and text building that every later module uses.

steps.title: Give a value a name and a type
steps.text: A variable is a name for a value. In C# the type comes first. int open = 4; creates a variable named open that holds whole numbers, and gives it 4. double holds numbers with a fraction, such as 2.5. string holds text in double quotes. bool holds true or false. Read = as "gets". A semicolon ends each statement, and statements run from top to bottom. A variable can get a new value later. open = open + 1; works out the right side first, then stores the result in open.

steps.title: Trace the count
steps.text: Read the example before running it. Console.WriteLine(value) prints the value on its own line. Predict all three lines.

steps.title: Run the board
steps.text: Run the example and compare it with your prediction. The first print sees 4. The assignment then gives open a new value, so the second print sees 5. opening still holds 4. The line int open = opening; copied the number, so the two names share nothing afterwards.

steps.title: Divide two whole numbers
steps.text: +, - and * work as in arithmetic. Division depends on the types. When both sides are int, / gives a whole number and drops the fraction, and % gives the remainder. Predict the three lines before running.

steps.title: Keep the fraction
steps.text: With two ints, 7 / 2 is 3 and 7 % 2 is the 1 left over. Line 5 stores done in a double. An int fits in a double with no extra code. Now exact / days has a double on one side, so the result keeps its fraction: 3.5, which is greater than 3. A bool prints as True or False. You can also convert in place with a cast: (double)done / days. Convert before dividing. (double)(done / days) divides the two ints first, so the fraction is already gone.

steps.title: Let the compiler pick the type, and build text
steps.text: var asks the compiler to work out the type from the first value (inference). var label = "Desk"; means exactly the same as string label = "Desk";. The type is still fixed. A $ before the opening quote makes an interpolated string: each {name} inside it is replaced by that value. Without the $, the braces are ordinary text. You can also join text with +.

steps.title: Predict a type error
steps.text: A variable's type decides what it can hold. Quoted digits are text, not a number. Read the example before checking it.

steps.title: Read the compiler error
steps.text: Check the example. CS0029 means the value on the right cannot be converted to the type on the left. Here "5" is a string and count is an int. The compiler stops before anything runs, so nothing prints. The message names the line, and that line is where to start reading.

steps.title: Show a delivery arriving
steps.text: The case boxes above the editor supply opening and arrivals. Each case uses different numbers, and your answer must work for all of them. Read only the lines that set a value. The using static line and the class around them are wrapping that the Classes module explains. Edit the starter, save, and compare both printed lines.

steps.title: Write two small answers
steps.text: Work from each prompt, then save. One answer needs a division that keeps its fraction. The other builds a text label.

steps.title: Repair a broken count
steps.text: Read the compiler message before editing. Trace the variable back to the line that gave it its type.

questions.prompt: What are the three output lines, in order?

choices.feedback: The first print runs before the assignment. opening kept its own copy of 4.
opening and open are separate variables. Changing open leaves opening at 4.
A line that already printed cannot change. The first print ran before the assignment.

questions.prompt: What are the three output lines, in order?

choices.feedback: done and days are both int, so / drops the fraction and gives 3.
Two ints divide to a whole number, the remainder is 1, and 3.5 is greater than 3.
exact is a double, so exact / days is 3.5, which is greater than 3.

choices.feedback: "5" is text. C# does not turn text into a number when you assign it.

choices.text: The compiler reports an error on line 2 and nothing runs.
choices.feedback: Line 2 tries to store a string in an int variable. That is CS0029.

choices.text: It prints 4, then stops with an error.
choices.feedback: The example never prints before line 2, and the compiler checks the whole file before running any of it.

tasks.title: Show a delivery arriving
tasks.prompt: opening is how many tasks were open and arrivals is how many just came in. Both are supplied whole numbers. The starter prints the opening count, then an out-of-date total. Give total its new value between the two print lines. With 6 open and 2 arriving, the output is 6 then 8, one number per line.
hints: Read the print lines from top to bottom. Which one should see the new value?
An assignment works out its right side first, then stores the result in the name on the left.
Between the prints, add arrivals to the current total and store the result back in total.

total must end as opening plus arrivals.

tasks.title: Split the hours evenly
tasks.prompt: hours is a supplied whole number of hours. people is a supplied whole number of people, at least 1. Declare a double named share that holds the hours split evenly between the people, keeping any fraction. With 7 hours and 2 people, share is 3.5.
hints: What does / give when both sides are int?
One side of the division must be a double before the division happens.
Store hours in a double variable first, or write (double)hours, then divide by people.
tasks.starter: double share = 0;
tasks.solution:
double exact = hours;
double share = exact / people;
checkLabels: share must be hours divided by people, with the fraction kept.
share must be a double.
tasks.feedback: Work the case with 7 hours and 2 people by hand. If your answer gives 3, the division happened between two ints.

tasks.title: Label a shelf
tasks.prompt: area is a supplied string and open is a supplied whole number. Declare a string named label in the form "Desk: 3 open": the area, a colon and a space, the number, a space, then the word open. Build it from the supplied values so it works for every case.
hints: Which parts of the label change from case to case, and which stay the same?
An interpolated string starts with $ before the opening quote.
Inside the $ string, put area and open in braces, and type the colon, the spaces and the word open as plain text.
tasks.starter: string label = "";
tasks.solution: string label = $"{area}: {open} open";
checkLabels: label must be the area, a colon and a space, the count, then the word open.
tasks.feedback: Compare your label with the expected text one character at a time. Check the $ before the quote and the spaces around the number.

tasks.title: Repair a broken count
tasks.prompt: The starter should work out how many tasks are still unfinished, but it does not compile. opening and done are supplied whole numbers. Read the compiler error, then repair the code so remaining is a whole number equal to opening minus done.
hints: The error names a line and two types. Which type does remaining have, and which line gave it that type?
var takes its type from the first value. "0" in quotes is a string.
Give remaining a number as its first value, so the result of the subtraction fits.
tasks.starter:
var remaining = "0";
remaining = opening - done;
tasks.solution:
var remaining = 0;
remaining = opening - done;
checkLabels: remaining must be a whole number equal to opening minus done.
tasks.feedback: remaining must hold a number, not text that looks like a number. Check the first value you give it, and the order of the subtraction.

tasks.prompt: seats is the number of seats in a room and booked is how many are taken. Both are supplied whole numbers, and at least one seat is free. Declare free with var as the number of free seats, and print it in the form "7 free". Then one more seat is booked: update free and print it again in the same form. With 12 seats and 5 booked, the output is 7 free then 6 free.
hints: How many lines must print, and what has changed between them?
Work out the free seats once, print, then store a new value in the same variable before printing again.
Start with var free = seats - booked; and print $"{free} free". Subtract 1 from free, then print the same text again.

Console.WriteLine($"{free} free");

lessons.title: Make a decision

outcomes.can: Predict which branch of an if, else if, else chain runs.
Combine conditions with &&, || and !.
Tell = from == and read the error when they are mixed up.
Handle two separate conditions, including empty text and zero.

lessons.intro: A program becomes useful when it can choose. This module covers if and else, the comparison operators, and combining true/false values with and, or and not.

steps.title: Compare, then choose
steps.text: A comparison produces a bool. open > limit is true when open is larger. The comparison operators are == (equal), != (not equal), <, <=, > and >=. An if statement runs its block only when the condition in the brackets is true. else if tries another condition when the ones above were false. else runs when none matched. Only one block in the chain runs. Two strings are equal with == when they hold the same characters, and "" is a real string with no characters in it.

steps.title: Which branch runs?
steps.text: Read the if chain and predict the first line of output.

steps.title: Follow the chain
steps.text: open is 3 and limit is 3. open > limit is false, so the first block is skipped. open == limit is true, so "full" prints and the else block is skipped. The order of the tests matters: the chain stops at the first true condition.

steps.title: Combine conditions
steps.text: && means and: true only when both sides are true. || means or: true when at least one side is true. ! means not: it flips true and false. Predict the last two lines.

steps.title: Work out each side
steps.text: urgent is true and blocked is false, so !blocked is true and urgent && !blocked is true. open >= 5 is false, but urgent is true, so the || is true. Work out each side first, then combine them.

steps.title: Predict a comparison error
steps.text: One character is missing from this condition. Read it before checking.

steps.title: Read the compiler error
steps.text: Check the example. A single = assigns. open = 3 stores 3 and produces an int, and an if needs a bool, so the compiler reports CS0029. To compare, write ==.

steps.title: Report the board status
steps.text: The case boxes supply open and limit. The starter handles one rule and has the edge wrong. Change it so every case gets the right status.

steps.title: Decide whether work can start
steps.text: Work from the prompt. Every case supplies a different mix of values.

The first test is false and the second is true, so its block runs.
else runs only when every condition above it was false.

open >= 5 is false, but || needs only one true side, and urgent is true.
!blocked flips false to true, so both sides of the && are true.

choices.text: It prints nothing, because the condition is false.

lessons.title: Give a calculation a name

outcomes.can: Trace separate calls and say which names are local to a method.
Write a method that returns different results on different paths.
Return a value and use one method from another.
Write a method from a description and keep the sign of its result.

lessons.intro: A method packages steps under a name so they can be used again with different values. This module covers parameters, return values and scope: which names exist where.

steps.title: Parts of a method
steps.text: A method has a return type, a name, parameters in brackets and a body in braces. In int AddHours(int hours, int extra), the method takes two ints and gives back an int. Parameters are names for the values a caller passes in. return sends a value back to the caller and ends the call. A method that gives nothing back has the return type void. When the body is a single expression you can write it with =>, as in int Twice(int n) => n * 2;. In exercises your methods go inside a class the checker supplies, so each one starts with public static. public lets other code call it. static means it is called by name, without an object. The Classes module explains both.

steps.title: Predict two calls
steps.text: Read the method and both calls before running.

steps.title: Trace the calls
steps.text: The first call passes 2 and 3, so hours is 2, extra is 3 and total is 5. The second call starts fresh with 1 and 0. total does not carry over: each call gets its own parameters and its own local variables. The method returns a value without printing it. The caller decides what to do with the result.

steps.title: Use a name outside its method
steps.text: The last line reads a name that was declared inside the method. Read the example before checking.

steps.title: Read the compiler error
steps.text: Check the example. CS0103 says the name total does not exist in the current context. total belongs to the body of AddHours (its scope). Code outside those braces cannot see it, even after a call. Use the value the method returns.

lessons.intro: Most programs work on many values at once. This module covers arrays, which have a fixed length, List<T>, which can grow, and the loops that visit each item.

steps.title: Arrays and loops
steps.text: An array holds a fixed number of values of one type. int[] minutes = { 30, 15, 45 }; creates an array of three ints. Positions (indexes) start at 0, so minutes[0] is 30 and minutes[2] is 45. minutes.Length is the number of items. Reading a position that does not exist, such as minutes[3], stops the program with an IndexOutOfRangeException. A foreach loop runs its block once for each item, in order. A variable declared before the loop can collect a result across the runs.

steps.title: Lists that grow
steps.text: A List<T> holds items of type T and can change size. new List<string>() creates an empty list of strings, and new List<int> { 4, 9 } creates one with two items already in it. Add appends an item. Count is the number of items, where an array uses Length. A for loop counts with a variable: for (int i = 0; i < titles.Count; i++) runs with i equal to 0, 1 and so on, and stops when i reaches Count. i++ adds 1 to i. Use for when you need the position, and foreach when you only need the item.

lessons.intro: A class groups data with the methods that work on it. This module covers properties, constructors and instance methods, and what happens when two variables refer to the same object.

steps.title: A class is a blueprint
steps.text: A class describes one kind of thing. new TaskCard("Pack", 30) creates an object from it. A property is a named value on each object. public string Title { get; private set; } can be read by any code and changed only inside the class. public int Minutes { get; } can be set only in the constructor. A property can also work out its value each time it is read: public bool Long => Minutes > 60;. The constructor has the same name as the class. It runs once, when the object is created, and gives the properties their first values. A method without static belongs to one object and uses that object's own properties.

A class variable holds a reference to an object, and the assignment copies that reference. card and same now refer to one object, so a change made through same is visible through card. This differs from int, where assignment copies the number itself. Describe then reads the current Title and Minutes of that one object.

lessons.title: Records, structs and copies

Predict == for records, structs and classes.

lessons.intro: Some types exist to carry data. This module covers records, which compare by value and are copied with with, and structs, which are copied on every assignment. It also shows how both differ from a class.

steps.title: A record carries data
steps.text: record Job(string Title, int Minutes); declares a record in one line. It has a constructor with those two parameters and a property for each. The properties can be set only when the record is created. To change something you make a copy: first with { Minutes = 45 } is a new Job with the same Title and a different Minutes. Two records are equal with == when all their values are equal. Printing a record shows its type name and values.

steps.title: Copy with a change
steps.text: second is made from first with one value changed. Predict the first line of output.

steps.title: Follow the copy
steps.text: with created a second Job and left first alone, so first.Minutes is still 30. The second line shows the copy: the same Title and the new Minutes. Nothing can change a Job after it is created, so code that holds one can rely on it.

steps.title: Value or reference
steps.text: A struct is a value type, like int. Assigning it copies the whole value, so Size b = a; gives b its own Width. A class is a reference type: assignment copies the reference and both names refer to one object. For == the rule also depends on the type. Records compare their values. Classes compare references, so two separate objects are not equal even when they hold the same data.

lessons.title: Handle a missing value

outcomes.can: Supply a fallback for a missing value with ??.

lessons.intro: Sometimes there is no value: a task with no owner, a card with no due date. C# calls that null. This module covers marking a value that may be missing, checking it before use, and supplying a fallback.

steps.title: null means no value
steps.text: null means a variable refers to nothing. string? owner = null; declares a string that may be missing. The ? after the type is a promise to readers and tools that null is allowed here, and editors use it to warn you when you use such a value without a check. Using a member of null, such as owner.Length, stops the program with a NullReferenceException. Test first with owner == null or owner != null. The ?? operator supplies a fallback: owner ?? "Unassigned" is owner when it has a value and "Unassigned" when it is null. The ?. operator reads a member only when there is a value. owner?.Length is null when owner is null, and no exception is thrown.

steps.title: Follow the operators

steps.title: Empty is not missing

steps.title: Keep real values
steps.text: "" is a real string, so ?? leaves it alone and the comparison prints True. The same holds for numbers. An int always has a value and can never be null. int? is a different type that holds either an int or null. due.HasValue is False while due is null. After due = 0; it holds a real 0, and due ?? -1 gives 0, not the fallback. Zero and empty text are values. Only null means missing.

outcomes.can: Build and update counts in a Dictionary.
Read a key that may be missing without stopping the program.
Collect unique values with a HashSet.

lessons.intro: A list finds items by position. A Dictionary finds a value by its key, and a HashSet keeps each value only once. This module covers both, including what happens when a key is missing.

steps.title: Find a value by its key
steps.text: A Dictionary<string, int> stores pairs: a string key and an int value for it. open["Ana"] = 2; stores 2 under the key "Ana", adding the key if it is new and replacing the value if it exists. open["Ana"] reads the value. Reading a key that is not there stops the program with a KeyNotFoundException. To be safe, ask first with ContainsKey, or use TryGetValue. open.TryGetValue("Cy", out int found) returns true and puts the value in found when the key exists, and returns false when it does not. The word out marks a variable that the method fills in. Count is the number of keys.

steps.text: Follow the value stored under "Ana". Predict the first two lines of output.

steps.title: Follow the dictionary
steps.text: Ana starts at 2. The fourth line reads 2, adds 1 and stores 3 back under the same key, so Ana is 3 and there are still only two keys. "Cy" was never added. ContainsKey returns False, and TryGetValue returns false, so the else block prints "no entry". Reading open["Cy"] directly would have stopped the program.

steps.title: Keep each value once
steps.text: A HashSet<string> holds values with no repeats. Add returns true when the value was new and false when the set already had it. Contains tests for a value, and Count is the number of different values.

steps.title: Follow the set

lessons.title: Query a collection

outcomes.can: Filter and transform a list with Where and Select.
Group items and total a value for each group.
Predict when a query runs and save its results at the right time.

lessons.intro: Filtering, transforming and counting come up so often that C# has a set of methods for them, called LINQ. This module covers lambdas, the most used LINQ methods, and the fact that a query does not run until its results are read.

steps.title: A lambda is a small method
steps.text: A lambda is a method written in place, without a name. task => !task.Done takes one task and returns whether it is still open. The part before => is the parameter and the part after it is the result. LINQ methods take lambdas. Where keeps the items for which the lambda returns true. Select replaces each item with the lambda's result. Count() counts the items, Any() says whether there is at least one, and Sum adds up a number taken from each item. The methods chain: the result of one is the input of the next.

steps.title: Filter, then transform
steps.text: open keeps the tasks that are not done. Predict the first two lines of output.

steps.title: Follow the query
steps.text: Where keeps Ship and Label, because Pack is done, so Count() is 2. Select then replaces each kept task with its Title, and string.Join puts a comma and a space between them. The order of the original list is preserved. GroupBy collects the items that share a key. Each group has a Key, here the owner, and can itself be counted or summed. Ana has two tasks and Ben has one.

steps.title: A query runs when it is read
steps.text: Where and Select do not do their work when you call them. They return a description of the work, called a query. Its type is IEnumerable<T>, which means something you can loop over. Lists and arrays fit that type too. The query runs each time something reads it: a foreach, Count(), or ToList(). This is called deferred execution. ToList() runs the query once and stores the results in a new list, which does not change afterwards. ToDictionary does the same into a dictionary, from one lambda for the key and one for the value.

When a result must not change later, end the query with ToList().

lessons.title: Share a contract

outcomes.can: Implement an interface and use the type through it.
Extend a class and override a method so the right version runs.
Write two types behind one interface and a method that works with both.

lessons.intro: Different types can often be used the same way: several places to read tasks from, several kinds of card. This module covers interfaces, which state what a type can do, and inheritance, where one type builds on another.

steps.title: An interface is a contract
steps.text: An interface lists members without bodies. interface ISource says that any source has a Name and a Count method. A class takes on the contract by naming the interface after a colon, as in class FixedSource : ISource, and must then provide every member. Having matching members is not enough: the class has to name the interface. A variable of type ISource can hold any object whose class implements it. Code written against ISource works with all of them, including classes written later.

steps.title: A class can build on another
steps.text: class UrgentNotice : Notice makes UrgentNotice a kind of Notice. It gets Title and Text from Notice (inheritance). : base(title) passes the title on to Notice's constructor. A method marked virtual in the base class may be replaced, and the derived class replaces it with override. Records can inherit the same way, for example record Arrived(int Count) : Update. A type marked abstract cannot be created itself. It exists only to be inherited from.

steps.title: Which Text runs?

steps.title: Follow the calls
steps.text: The loop calls Name and Count through ISource and never needs to know the class. Each object answers with its own version. The same holds for notice.Text(). The variable's type is Notice, but the object is an UrgentNotice, and with virtual and override the object's own version runs, so the line is "Ship!". Without override, the derived method would only hide the base one, and a call through a Notice variable would run the base version.

outcomes.can: Trace which arm of a switch expression matches a value.

lessons.intro: Code often has to ask two questions at once: what kind of value is this, and what is inside it? Pattern matching answers both in one step. This module covers the is test, switch expressions, type patterns and property patterns, using the tracker's updates as data.

steps.title: Test a type and name the result
steps.text: A pattern is a test that a value either matches or does not. The simplest is a type pattern. update is Finished f asks whether update is a Finished record. When it is, f is that same object seen as a Finished, so f.Title is available. A switch expression tries several patterns in order and produces a value. Write the value to test, the word switch, then the arms in braces. Each arm is pattern => result, with a comma between arms. The first arm that matches wins. The discard _ matches anything, so it goes last.

steps.title: Follow two notices
steps.text: Read the method and both calls before running. Choose the two output lines in order.

steps.title: Follow the arms
steps.text: Describe is called twice. new Waiting(0) matches the first arm and returns "Place 0". The arm tests the type, so a Place of 0 is handled like any other number. new Finished("Pack") does not match the first arm, matches the second and returns its Title. The last arm runs only for a Notice type that the arms above do not name. Without it the compiler warns that the switch does not handle every input (CS8509), and a value that matches no arm throws SwitchExpressionException when the program runs.

steps.title: Test what is inside
steps.text: A property pattern tests values inside an object. { Minutes: 0 } matches when the Minutes property equals 0. A relational pattern compares: { Minutes: < 30 } matches any value below 30. One pattern can test several properties, as in { Urgent: true, Minutes: > 60 }. A property pattern can also follow a type, as in Finished { Minutes: 0 } f. Order matters because the first match wins, so put the most specific arm first.

steps.title: Which arm wins?
steps.text: More than one arm can match the same job. Read the arms from the top and predict the first call's result.

steps.title: Read the arms in order
steps.text: Job(0, true) matches the first arm, so it is "empty" even though it is urgent. Job(10, true) is not 0 but is below 30, so it is "short". Job(45, true) fails both Minutes tests and reaches the Urgent arm. Job(45, false) falls through to the discard. If the Urgent arm moved to the top, the first three results would all become "long and urgent".

steps.title: Read the compiler error

steps.title: Throw and catch
steps.text: An exception is an object that reports a failure. throw new ArgumentException("Minutes cannot be negative."); stops the current method at once and passes the exception to its caller. If nothing catches it, the program stops. A try block marks code that may fail, and a catch block after it runs only when an exception of the named type is thrown inside the try. catch (FormatException) catches that type and no other. Naming a variable, as in catch (ArgumentException error), lets you read error.Message. Some built-in methods throw: int.Parse("soon") throws a FormatException because the text is not a number.

steps.title: A Task is a result that comes later

A method that uses await must be marked async, and its return type is Task or Task<T>. Inside it you return the plain value, and C# wraps it in the task. lessons.intro: A check calls code with a known input and compares what comes back with what should come back. This module covers reading a failed check, choosing the input that exposes a bug, and writing a check of your own.

steps.title: Expected and actual
steps.text: Every check has an input, an expected result and an actual result. The expected result comes from the rule the code is meant to follow. The actual result is what the code returned. When they differ, the check has failed, and the input tells you which call to trace. The most useful inputs sit at an edge, where the rule changes its answer. For "three or more", the edge is exactly 3. A bug at an edge is easy to miss with inputs far away from it.

steps.title: Find the failing input
steps.text: AtLimit should return true when count has reached the limit or passed it. Predict the three lines, then decide which call shows the bug.

steps.title: Compare with the rule
steps.text: The rule expects True, True, False. The code prints True, False, False. Only the second call disagrees, and it is the one at the edge: 3 has reached a limit of 3, but the code uses >, which is false for equal values. The calls with 4 and 2 give the right answer with either operator, so they cannot tell the faulty code from the fixed code.

steps.title: A check is code too
steps.text: A method can receive another method as a parameter. Func<int, int, bool> is the type of a method that takes two ints and returns a bool. The last type in the list is the return type. A lambda such as (count, limit) => count >= limit fits it. A check written this way takes a candidate, calls it with chosen inputs, and returns true only when every result matches what is expected. A good check returns true for correct code and false for the faulty versions you know about. A check kept to make sure a fixed bug stays fixed is called a regression check.

The second candidate returns false at the edge, so the check returns False. Without the (3, 3) case both candidates would pass, and the check would be worthless for this bug.

steps.title: Read the request before writing
steps.text: An import audit reads rows and reports how many were accepted, how many repeated an accepted Id, and how many were invalid. The three counts measure different things, and every row belongs to exactly one of them. Before writing code, take two or three small inputs and work out the report by hand. Those become your first checks. Decide the order of your tests too: whether a row is invalid has to be settled before asking whether it is a repeat.

tasks.title: Audit a task import
tasks.prompt:
Row, AuditReport and the row readers are supplied. Write three methods.

1. public static AuditReport Summarize(List<Row> rows). A row is invalid when its Id is empty or its Title is empty. A valid row whose Id was already accepted is a duplicate. Every other row is accepted. Return the three counts and a Status: "empty" when there are no rows, "clean" when every row was accepted, and "review" otherwise. An invalid row does not use up its Id.

2. public static async Task<AuditReport> AuditAsync(IRowReader reader). Read the rows exactly once and return their summary. When the reader throws InvalidOperationException, return a report with the Status "unavailable" and three counts of 0.

3. public static bool SummarizeCheck(Func<List<Row>, AuditReport> candidate). A regression check for Summarize. Return true for a correct candidate, and false for a faulty one that counts duplicates as accepted.
hints: Work out the report by hand for three rows where the second repeats the first Id. What are the three counts?
Test whether a row is invalid before asking whether its Id was seen, and record an Id only when its row is accepted.
For the check, pass rows that contain a duplicate and compare the candidate's report with the exact report you worked out by hand.
checkLabels: Two valid rows with different Ids must give a clean report with 2 accepted.
No rows must give an empty report.
A row that repeats an accepted Id must be counted as 1 duplicate, not as accepted.
A row with an empty Id and a row with an empty Title must both be invalid.
Two rows with empty Ids are both invalid. Neither is a duplicate of the other.
An invalid row must not use up its Id for a later valid row.
AuditAsync must return the summary of the rows it read.
An unavailable reader must give the Status "unavailable" with three counts of 0.
AuditAsync must read the rows exactly once.
A correct candidate must pass your regression check.
A candidate that counts duplicates as accepted must fail your regression check.
